# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# A Careful Reading of the Two-Year Follow-up

This is a strong follow-up, and it answers several open questions directly:

- With log-measured hours, randomisation and a two-year horizon, the per-hour gain in case-processing offices persists at a reduced size (+8.5%).
- The meta-analysis's "no decay" claim rested entirely on uncontrolled studies using scheduled hours.
- The counter arm failed in practice.

There are four problems:

1. The log-hours measure doesn't reconcile with the meetings data.
2. Two control offices cutting their own meetings contaminate the estimate of decay.
3. The mediation result is described too strongly.
4. The meetings hypothesis was "confirmed" on the same offices that generated it.

## The numbers mostly check out

- **Output per hour.** 0.966 / 0.88 gives +9.8% on timesheets, and 0.966 / 0.89 gives +8.5% on logs. Both are correct.
- **Decline.** 12.5% falling to 9.8% is a 22% decline, so "about a quarter" is fair.
- **Halden continuers.** 34.9 / 40.3 is a 13.4% fall in hours, and 96.8 / 0.866 gives +11.8%. Both are correct.
- **Mediation shares.** 47 + 18 + 35 = 100.
- **Counter staffing.** Restoring hours with the 9-month per-hour gain implies 1 / (0.83 × 1.067) ≈ 1.13, about 13% more staff. That is consistent with the county's 12%. The estimated 9% rise in cost per contact is lower than a 12% rise in staff would suggest. Savings from fewer sick days might explain the gap, but the paper doesn't say how it was derived.

## Problems

**1. The log-hours measure doesn't reconcile with the meetings data.**
Log-in time is described as recording "time staff are working on cases". On that definition it excludes meetings.

| Treated offices, relative to control | Change (hours per week) |
|---|---|
| Total hours (timesheets, −12% of ~37.9) | about −4.5 |
| Recurring meetings (−3.5 treated vs −0.2 control) | about −3.3 |
| Implied non-meeting time | about −1.2, roughly −4% of ~30.5 |

Casework time measured by logs should therefore have fallen by roughly 4% or less, not 11%.

- Either the logs capture more than casework, such as being logged in during meetings, or one set of figures is wrong.
- This determines what the headline result means:
  - **If logs measure total working time**, the meetings pathway is close to an accounting identity: moving hours from meetings to casework raises output per hour by construction. That is a valid finding ("removing low-value time"), but it is not a separate productivity mechanism.
  - **If logs measure casework time only**, the per-casework-hour gain implies a genuine efficiency effect, and the 11% fall is hard to explain.

The paper calls logs the "stricter" measure, but that depends on which reading is correct. The authors need to state what the logs capture and reconcile the three figures.

**2. Contamination of the control group may account for part of the "decay".**
The "unplanned observation" is presented as a side note. It matters more than that:

- Two of seven control offices cut meetings at month 15 and raised output per hour by 4.1%.
- That alone lifts the control average by roughly 1.2% over months 15–21.
- This is of the same order as the 2.7-point decline from 12.5% to 9.8%.

Some of the apparent fading may be the controls improving rather than the treatment effect weakening. The trial is therefore under-estimating the effect of the full package relative to an untouched control. The authors should report the 24-month estimate both excluding these two offices and with an adjustment for them. They should also note that the trial itself plausibly prompted the audit, which is a form of spillover.

**3. "Confirms" overstates what a mediation analysis can show.**
The Limitations correctly note that mediation assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediator and outcome. The Summary still says the test "confirms" that meetings "account for" 47%. The obvious confounder is manager quality, which plausibly drives both meeting cuts and productivity. With 7 treated offices, the 28–66% interval is notably narrow. The analysis supports "consistent with a substantial meetings pathway", not confirmation.

**4. The registered test reuses the offices that generated the hypothesis.**

- Registering at month 11, before 24-month outcomes, is good practice, and later data from months 10–24 is new data.
- However, the hypothesis came from these same 7 treated offices.
- "A larger sample of office-months" adds repeated observations, not independent units. The effective sample is still 14 offices.
- The test reduces the post-hoc concern but does not remove it. Replication in a different employer is needed before calling the pathway established.

**5. A meetings baseline appears without explanation.**
The nine-month report said meeting data were collected only in month six. This report gives baseline figures of 7.4 and 7.2 hours. If these come from retrospective calendar extraction, the paper should say so and describe what that extraction covers. This baseline is what makes the "reduction" claim valid now, when it wasn't at nine months.

**6. Inference with few clusters remains unaddressed.**
There are still 14 clusters, with no statement of the method used (for example, a wild-cluster bootstrap or randomisation inference). The main +8.5% interval is probably robust, given how far its lower bound is from zero. The mediation intervals are more vulnerable.

**7. Backlog and cost data are still missing.**

- Two years is long enough to show whether queues built up. Deadline compliance and backlog size are still not reported.
- Cost is analysed for the counter arm but not for case-processing. There, output per FTE is −3.4% at unchanged pay, plus overtime, offset in part by 27% fewer sick days and roughly half the resignations. A cost-per-case figure would directly answer the county's question.

**8. The Halden follow-up is more selected than stated.**

- Only 14 of the 23 record-holding organisations responded, adding a 39% non-response layer. The organisations are survivors three times over, not twice.
- "Upper bound" isn't strictly justified. Without a comparison group, secular trends over 24 months could push the estimate either way.
- The baseline of 40.3 hours is identical to Varga and Holm's 27-organisation figure. That may be a coincidence, but it is worth confirming that it was recomputed for these 11 organisations.
- A Halden author co-authors this section. The framing is appropriately cautious, but the potential conflict is worth noting.

**9. One reversion complicates the binary classification of work.**
The marketing agency that reverted cited client deadlines. Marketing would be coded discretionary, but external deadlines and client responsiveness give it coverage-like properties. This supports the meta-analysis's caveat that the binary is a simplification.

## What it gets right

- **The rebuttal of "entirely an artifact".** Varden at 24 months meets every standard Varga and Holm recommended: record-based output, actual hours, a randomised comparison and at least 18 months of follow-up. It still finds +8.5% (3.4 to 13.8).
- **The rebuttal of "no decay".** Showing that all four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours confirms that the meta-analysis's duration claim was unsupported.
- **Candour about decline.** The authors report the fall from 12.5% to 9.8% openly, and they reject the more flattering scheduled-hours figures.
- **The hours-versus-reorganisation question.** The authors correctly say the trial cannot tell whether reorganisation alone would capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what forces and sustains it.
- **The counter arm.** Waits of 7.3 minutes against 4.0, now properly compared with control, and the county's decision to end the arm settle the coverage-bound question as far as one employer can.

## Where the evidence now stands

| Claim | Status after the follow-up |
|---|---|
| Halden's +23.4% | Inflated. Corrected estimates in Halden subsets are about +11–12%, and those organisations are heavily selected. |
| "Entirely an artifact" | Refuted by the best available study. |
| Per-hour gain in discretionary work | About +8–10% at two years in one randomised trial, with output per employee about −3%. |
| Durability | The gain is partly durable. Some decay is likely, but its size is uncertain because of control contamination. |
| Coverage-bound work | Fails without extra staff: about 12% more staff and an estimated 9% higher cost per contact. |
| Meetings mechanism | Plausibly a large share of the gain, pending reconciliation of the log-hours figures and replication elsewhere. |
| Gains without cutting hours | An open question. Two contaminated control offices hint that part is available, but there is no direct test. |

The natural next study is a three-arm trial: a reduced-hours arm, a reorganisation-only arm (meeting audit with unchanged hours), and a control arm. That would separate the effect of cutting hours from the effect of the reorganisation it seems to prompt.
